top.headline: As Democrats Prepare to Take Power, Trump's DOJ Escalates Threats to Prosecute Them
top.blurb: Trump is pushing a new attempt to indict the "Seditious Six" Democrats who urged troops to refuse illegal orders, after a grand jury effort reportedly failed in February, while a US Attorney in Texas has implied possible charges against Sens. Blumenthal, Slotkin and Warren over their oversight work. A White House Counsel letter also warned incoming Oversight Chair Robert Garcia that Democratic investigations of the administration could themselves amount to criminality.

top.headline: Sean Duffy Blames Decades of Underinvestment for a Ground Stop That Happened on His Watch
top.blurb: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize for Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, telling Meet the Press he "can't apologize for what was passed off to us." But Congress gave the FAA $12.5 billion for modernization in 2025, and lawmakers say only about a third of it has been spent under an administration that has now run the agency for nearly two years.

top.headline: US Prosecutors Seek 24 Years for the Indian National Who Plotted to Kill a Sikh Separatist on US Soil
top.blurb: Nikhil Gupta, who pleaded guilty to paying a man he believed was a hitman $15,000 to kill Sikhs for Justice's Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, faces sentencing Friday after US prosecutors asked for 24 years, calling his conduct "brutal" and "brazen." Prosecutors allege Gupta worked with a RAW official, a claim New Delhi calls "fabricated and malicious" even as a separate US civil suit now names NSA Ajit Doval and former RAW chief Samant Goel.

top.headline: 935 Shutdowns in 14 Years: A Data Portrait of How India Switches Off the Internet
top.blurb: Software Freedom Law Center data analyzed by Newslaundry shows Jammu and Kashmir alone accounts for nearly half of India's 935 recorded internet shutdowns since 2012, with 70% imposed preventively rather than in response to any disruption. India has had more shutdowns than any other country since 2019, and the piece finds oversight committees dominated by the executive with no cap on how long a suspension can run.

top.headline: After Its Own Reporting Triggered the Complaint, NCW Orders a Probe Into a Tamil Nadu MLA Accused of Harassing a District Collector
top.blurb: The National Commission for Women has asked Tamil Nadu's DGP for an inquiry, citing a TNM report, into allegations that Kallakurichi MLA C Arul Vignesh sent obscene messages to and misbehaved with District Collector JE Padmaja. Vignesh denies the allegations and has offered a blood test, while officials say a formal POSH complaint would need to come from Padmaja herself, who has not filed one.

top.headline: Israel's Would-Be Coalition-Builder Says Netanyahu Must Go 'Immediately' Over Alleged Vote-Rigging Raids
top.blurb: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel's next government, said Netanyahu "cannot remain at the helm of government for even one more minute" after reports that his chief of staff triggered warrantless raids on three Arab-led party members based on an intelligence tip later found baseless. Shin Bet's chief had separately sought to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli lawmakers on election day, a request the attorney general's office rejected.

top.headline: ASEAN and China Reach 80% of a South China Sea Deal — and Stop There
top.blurb: Talks in Manila missed the Philippines' year-end deadline for a South China Sea code of conduct, with the Philippines' foreign minister saying a draft is "tentatively" 80% agreed but core questions — chiefly whether the code would be legally binding — remain open after two decades of negotiation. ASEAN separately extended its ban on Myanmar's junta leader attending summits over stalled progress on the bloc's 2021 peace plan.

top.headline: India Claw Back the ODI Decider to Win the Series 3-1 After New Zealand's Record Blowout
top.blurb: India bowled out New Zealand for 22 runs short while defending 209 at the Bay Oval, with Arshdeep Singh taking 3/30 and Axar Patel closing it out, to win the fifth ODI by 22 runs and the series 3-1 — four days after New Zealand's 244-run demolition in the same ground had leveled it. India now add this to a 3-2 T20I series win before the two sides shift to Tests on November 19.

more.headline: Hridoy's Second Century in as Many Tests Rescues Bangladesh After Rabada's Five-For
more.blurb: Bangladesh slumped to 22/3 before Towhid Hridoy's 137 and an unbeaten 92 from Litton Das built a 206-run partnership, their highest for any wicket against South Africa, to reach 327/6 at stumps on day one in Johannesburg despite Kagiso Rabada's 5/51.

top.headline: A Patna Childhood, a Shortwave Radio, and the Night R.D. Burman Got a Name
top.blurb: In this excerpt from his memoir Matinee Magic, Anirudha Bhattacharjee recalls a 1970s Patna evening — a power cut, a song drifting from a music shop, a Lata Mangeshkar track on Radio Ceylon — that ends with an announcer finally crediting the tune to R.D. Burman. It's a small, sensory piece about how a composer's name reaches a listener long after his music already has.

bengal.headline: A Birbhum Shooting Suspect Is Killed in Custody — Bengal's Fifth Such Gunfight Death Since the BJP Took Power
bengal.blurb: Ratan Sheikh, accused of shooting a constable in Santiniketan on Friday, was killed in an alleged gunfight in Birbhum on Sunday — the fifth time since May that a crime suspect has died in a police shooting Suvendu Adhikari's government describes as self-defence.

bengal.headline: A Thank-You to the Chief Minister in a Pre-Primary Textbook Draws Teachers' Objections
bengal.blurb: Revised textbooks reaching Bengal schools for 2027 credit Suvendu Adhikari and the education minister for their "guidance," prompting a teachers' association to argue that public money shouldn't fund political acknowledgements in children's books.

travel.headline: Camera Traps Catch One of Southeast Asia's Rarest Cats Hunting by Day in a Borneo Mangrove
travel.blurb: Nearly three years of camera-trapping in a proposed Sarawak protected forest recorded the endangered flat-headed cat just 59 times, mostly on slightly raised, palm-dominated ground — and active by day as well as night, upending its reputation as strictly nocturnal.

happy.headline: An Unknown Altdorfer Hung in a Swiss Living Room for 70 Years. It May Be Worth $6.6 Million.
happy.blurb: A nine-by-eight-inch forest scene bought in 1957 from an Austrian aristocratic collection sat unrecognized in private Swiss hands for decades until scholars confirmed it this year as the third known oil landscape by Albrecht Altdorfer, the Renaissance painter credited with inventing landscape as its own subject rather than a backdrop for myth or scripture. No work by Altdorfer has come to market since 1980; this one — a dense, unpeopled forest with a rainbow caught just after a storm — goes to Sotheby's London on December 9, where museums are expected to compete for it.

tech_top.headline: Treasury Secretary Tells Nvidia's Board to Hire an Outsider — and Gives It 10 Days to Prove It Followed Chip-Export Law
tech_top.blurb: Scott Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for Jensen Huang's successor and demanded it show within 10 days that the company complied with US export controls, including whether it pushed chip sales to China to juice revenue. The board has reportedly discussed Arm's Rene Haas as a candidate, while Huang's own allies lobby for his return.
tech_top.pm_note: A cabinet official setting a public compliance deadline, rather than quiet regulatory back-and-forth, shows how fast an export-control question can turn into a governance crisis that outruns a company's own succession plan.

tech_top.headline: A Delhi Chip Startup Raises $24M to Fuse Camera and AI Onto One Sensor
tech_top.blurb: Bharat Semi raised a $24M seed round led by Info Edge, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures to build image sensors that combine capture, processing and AI on a single chip, which co-founder Vrinda Kapoor says could cut system costs by 70% versus separate sensor-plus-processor setups. The five-year-old, pre-revenue startup already has design wins with General Atomics and Kaynes Semicon, with commercial production targeted for 2027.
tech_top.pm_note: Collapsing three separate chips into one is a classic vertical-integration bet: it can undercut incumbents on cost, but it also means the startup now owns performance problems — in sensing, compute, and AI — that used to be three different vendors' to fix.

tech_more.headline: Apple Launches a Health Chatbot Study Built on Medical Journals, Not General AI Chat
tech_more.blurb: Apple's new Health AI Study app, built with OpenEvidence, answers health questions by drawing on sources like NEJM, JAMA and Nature, and aims to enroll up to 200,000 U.S. iPhone users over a year to study how people use and judge AI health answers.

tech_101.text: A semiconductor startup that designs chips but pays another factory to actually manufacture them — the model Bharat Semi uses to compete with far larger, vertically integrated rivals without building its own multi-billion-dollar fab.

An AI model restricted to answer from vetted sources like peer-reviewed medical journals, instead of generating a free-form answer the way a general chatbot does — Apple's bet that narrower, sourced answers build more trust for health questions.

science.headline: SpaceX Catches a Returning Starship in Midair for the First Time
science.blurb: Saturday's Starship flight orbited Earth 14 times, released 26 Starlink satellites, and was caught by the launch tower's mechanical arms on return — the first time SpaceX has recovered a Starship spacecraft from orbit, even after the booster's early engine shutdown forced a self-destruct over the Gulf of Mexico. NASA is counting on the reusability this demonstrates for Artemis Moon landings later this decade.

science.headline: A Color-Changing Molecule Can Spot Invisible Mercury in Seconds, Using Just a Phone Camera
science.blurb: Istanbul Technical University researchers built a selenium-based sensor molecule that turns yellow-to-green and glows under near-infrared light when it binds mercury, detecting the metal down to roughly one part in a quarter-billion within 10 seconds. Photographed with an ordinary smartphone camera, it worked on drinking water, lake water and produce, offering a cheaper alternative to lab-only mercury testing.

science.headline: One Endangered Penguin, Two Opposite Fates — and a Population Count That Was Hiding Both
science.blurb: A three-year drone census of erect-crested penguins found the Bounty Islands' colony unchanged in 25 years while the larger Antipodes Islands colony has fallen more than 40% since 1995, likely from rising skua predation, storm damage and poorer feeding grounds. Researchers warn that treating the species as one population, rather than two, would mask the Antipodes decline behind the Bounty colony's stability.

science.headline: Why the Same Nitrate-Rich Food Doesn't Carry the Same Cancer Risk — the Answer May Be Vitamin C
science.blurb: A University of Waterloo model of digestion found that vitamin C eaten alongside nitrates or nitrites can interfere with the stomach reaction that forms cancer-linked compounds, which may explain why nitrate-rich vegetables like spinach — which also carry vitamin C — haven't shown the same risk as cured meats. The findings come from simulation only; the researchers stress human studies are still needed.

philosophy.headline: Astronomy Keeps Calling Stars and Dust a 'Nuisance' in Its Rush to Answer the Big Questions
philosophy.blurb: Astrophysicist Dylan Jow argues his field has been absorbed into physics, so dark matter and the early universe get funded and published while dust, gas and ordinary stars get treated as noise to subtract from the data. He calls this a historically contingent choice rather than a fixed hierarchy, and urges astronomers back toward the messier, more human question of where we came from.

philosophy.headline: Why the Wall Between Church and State Isn't About Subject Matter at All
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Neil Van Leeuwen and legal scholar Jacob Eisler argue that religious belief is a distinct mental attitude — voluntary, insulated from evidence, and confined to sacred settings — not a different subject from ordinary factual belief. That psychological split, they argue, is exactly what justifies letting citizens hold religious views privately while requiring public policy to rest on evidence everyone can contest.

philosophy.headline: At 84, After Two Heart Surgeries in 12 Days, a Zen Teacher Reckons With an Unfinished Life
philosophy.blurb: Physician Ben Daitz traces his friend Roshi Joan Halifax's path from a childhood bout of polio, through civil-rights activism and a breakdown during LSD research with dying patients, to the Zen center and end-of-life teaching she built from it. She emerges wary of her own need for approval and resistant to the idea of a finished legacy, preferring work she still considers incomplete.

philosophy_101.text: Something a study measures only to subtract it out of the way, like cosmic dust blurring a telescope's view of the early universe. The astronomy essay argues too much of the sky has quietly been reclassified this way.

The particular way a belief is held, not just its content. Two people can affirm the same claim, but one holds it as revisable fact and the other as faith immune to evidence — a difference this essay says is what actually separates religion from everything else government touches.
